international.title: Tories welcome Louise Haigh’s hint government could adopt their plan to scrap Natural England – UK politics live
international.summary: First secretary of state has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh The full text of Louise Haigh ’s speech to the CBI is now on the Cabinet Office’s website . In her speech to the CBI, Louise Haigh , the first secretary of state, delivered one of the most detailed explanations we have had from a minister as to what Andy Burnham means when he calls for more public control of utilities. Now I know the word privatisation can start an argument. So let me be precise. This is not about whether markets work. They do. Where there is genuine competition, as in telecoms, markets have given consumers choice and kept prices low while delivering infrastructure. The social licence to operate must be won every day by building trust and having the best value, product or service. Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive, supported by our strong, independent Competition and Markets Authority. To make the experiment work, successive governments leant on regulation, first to try to recreate competition from monopolies through a spreadsheet; then to manage what private markets would never price on their own, like the spare capacity that keeps the lights on; then to deliver social policy, treated as a free good because it went on the bill, not the budget. Ofgem now has six times the staff it had in the early 2000s, almost three times the administrative budget in real terms, and a rule book more than six times longer. We’ve got a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one. Not consumers, not investors. When you prioritise everything, you prioritise nothing. Continue reading...
